headline: Showers ease tonight, then wet, windy weather Monday through Wednesday, with more rain possible late week.
summary: Western Washington gets a brief break tonight as showers taper off and a ridge of high pressure, an area of higher air pressure that brings drier weather, moves through. Highs are expected in the mid to upper 50s. A new front arrives Monday, with rain reaching the coast in the afternoon and spreading slowly inland into the evening, along with southerly winds gusting 20 to 30 mph, and up to 35 mph on the coast and Whidbey Island. Tuesday looks wetter and windier, as a long plume of moisture moves down through the region, with most of the rain aimed at the coast and Olympic Peninsula and gusts of 35 to 45 mph possible along the coast and from Whidbey Island northward. Rain and wind continue into Wednesday morning, and forecasters expect high-elevation snow in the mountains during this stretch. Scattered showers continue Wednesday and Thursday, with Wednesday highs in the low 60s. Minor coastal flooding from high tides may be possible Wednesday morning in the San Juans and Whatcom County. Friday into Saturday, an upper-level low, a area of low pressure high in the atmosphere, near British Columbia is expected to pull moisture toward the region, bringing widespread rain and breezy winds into the weekend, though forecasters are still uncertain about this system and will refine it as it nears. River flooding is not expected in the next seven days, but repeated rain will soak the soils. If an atmospheric river, a long band of moisture, stalls over the area late next week into next weekend, the Skokomish River could need watching; forecasters call this a possibility, not an expectation.
changes: Earlier discussions today mentioned possible record highs Wednesday and a stronger atmospheric river Friday into Saturday, but the latest drops the record language and describes Wednesday highs only in the low 60s. The latest also describes the Friday-into-Saturday system as an upper-level low pulling in moisture and ties the Skokomish flood concern to a possible stall rather than a defined river of moisture.
